breakfast.name: Dholl Puri
ingredients: Filling: ground yellow split peas, cumin, turmeric
instructions: Boil and grind split peas
Mix into dough
Roll thin and cook on tawa
Serve with curry and chutneys
breakfast.description: Thin flatbread stuffed with spiced split peas — Mauritius's street food icon.

breakfast.name: Roti Chaud (Hot Flatbread)
instructions: Make dough, rest
Roll thin, cook on tawa
Brush with oil, fold
Serve with curry

breakfast.name: Mine Frit (Fried Noodles)
instructions: Boil noodles briefly — rinse under cold water to stop cooking
Fry garlic, ginger in hot oil
Add noodles — fry over very high heat
Add soy sauce, oyster sauce — the heat must be high or noodles become soggy
Toss with vegetables — quick, high-heat
Push to side, scramble eggs in the same wok
Mix through
Scallions at the end
Mine frit is Mauritius' Chinese-influenced fried noodle — the Chinese community (Hakka) brought it
One of the most popular breakfast and lunch dishes in Mauritius
The Chinese-Creole fusion character of Mauritius shows in every mine frit stall
Found at 'dholl puri' street vendors alongside the Indian flatbreads
breakfast.description: Mauritius' Chinese-Hakka fried noodle — egg noodles with vegetables and eggs tossed in a screaming hot wok with soy and oyster sauce. The Hakka Chinese community (one of Mauritius' five major ethnic groups) contributed mine frit to the national food culture. Found at street stalls alongside Indian dholl puri — the Mauritius multi-ethnic street food tableau.

breakfast.name: Roti Chapati with Achard
ingredients: Achard (Mauritius pickled vegetable relish: green mango or mixed vegetables)
instructions: Chapati: mix atta, water, salt into soft dough
Rest 20 minutes
Roll thin circles
Dry fry on a hot tava until both sides have brown spots and puff
Brush with ghee
Serve with achard — the sharp, mustard-seed pickle is the Mauritian accompaniment
Achard is Mauritius' pickle — sliced green mango or mixed vegetables pickled with mustard seeds, turmeric, and vinegar
The Indian flatbread-pickle breakfast is the Indian-Mauritius morning
The word 'achard' comes from French 'achards' (pickles) brought by the French colonizers from Indian trade
So achard is: an Indian-origin pickle, carried by French colonizers, grown Mauritian
breakfast.description: Mauritius' chapati-and-pickle breakfast — Indian-style whole wheat flatbread served with achard, Mauritius' signature pickled vegetable relish. Achard's etymology reveals Mauritius' layered history: an Indian-origin pickle method (mustard seed, turmeric) that traveled with French colonial trade, then became irreversibly Mauritian. The Indian morning in a French-named pickle.

lunch.name: Octopus Curry
instructions: Tenderize and clean octopus
Sauté onion, garlic, ginger, spices
Add tomatoes and coconut milk
Add octopus, simmer 25 min
lunch.description: Tender octopus in spiced coconut curry.

lunch.name: Mine Frit (Fried Noodles)
instructions: Cook noodles, drain
Stir-fry protein with garlic, ginger
Add vegetables, noodles, sauces
Toss until well coated

lunch.name: Biryani Mauricien
ingredients: Biryani masala (cumin, coriander, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, bay)
Potato (a Mauritius addition — not standard Indian biryani)
Fried onion, fresh mint, cilantro for garnish
instructions: Marinate meat in yogurt and spices — at least 2 hours
Par-boil rice until 70% cooked — rinse
Layer: fried onion on bottom, then spiced meat, then par-cooked rice, then saffron water
The Mauritius addition: par-cooked potato cubes between the meat and rice layers
Cover tightly, cook on very low heat (dum) — the steam cooks everything through
The potato absorbs the meat juices and the biryani spice aroma
This is the biryani identifier: potato in biryani is a Mauritius/Kolkata regional addition
Open at the table — the fragrance of steam escaping is part of the ritual
Biryani mauricien is served at every Mauritian celebration — weddings, Eid, family gatherings
The potato layer is the Mauritian signature — Indian biryani masters from outside often argue about it
lunch.description: Mauritius' celebration rice — basmati biryani cooked dum-style with a layer of potato between the meat and rice (a Mauritius/Kolkata regional signature that other biryani traditions argue about). The potato absorbs all the meat juices and spice fragrance. Every Mauritian wedding has biryani. The potato is the identity marker.

lunch.name: Boulettes (Street Dumplings)
ingredients: Soy sauce, chili sauce at table
instructions: Boulettes are Mauritius' street dumplings — small balls of minced meat or fish
Mix filling with spring onion, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, egg white to bind
Form into small balls — walnut-sized
Poach in clear broth — they cook through in the broth
Serve in the broth with rice noodles
The clear broth is always present
The Chinese origin is obvious — this is the Hakka meatball soup adapted for Mauritius
Served from street carts — the boulette lady with a steaming pot is a Mauritius street food image
Soy sauce, chili sauce at the table — each person seasons their own bowl
The boulettes concept adapted to every ingredient available in Mauritius — fish, chicken, beef, tofu
lunch.description: Mauritius' street dumpling soup — small minced meat or fish balls poached in clear broth, served with rice noodles and chili sauce. Directly from the Hakka Chinese community's culinary tradition. Boulette vendors with steaming pots are one of the most recognizable Mauritius street food images. The clear broth + chewy dumpling + chili sauce is the Mauritian street bowl.

dinner.name: Rougaille (Tomato Stew)
instructions: Sauté onion, garlic, ginger, thyme
Add tomatoes, cook to sauce
Add sausages or fish
Simmer 15 min
Serve with rice
dinner.description: Creole tomato stew — the backbone of Mauritian cooking.

dinner.name: Biryani Mauricien
instructions: Marinate chicken in yogurt and spices
Parboil rice
Layer chicken, rice, fried onion, saffron milk
Cover, cook on low 30 min
Serve with chutney

dinner.name: Rougaille (Creole Tomato Sauce)
instructions: Fry onion in oil until golden
Add garlic, ginger — the Mauritian rougaille always has ginger, which distinguishes it
Add tomatoes — fresh and roughly chopped
The tomatoes break down into a sauce — 15 minutes on medium heat
Add thyme, bay leaf, whole dried chili (for heat but not intense)
The rougaille should be saucy but not too liquid — it reduces
Season with salt
Rougaille is Mauritius' Creole sauce — the base for everything
Rougaille de saucisses (smoked sausage rougaille) is the most popular version
But fish, chicken, or served plain with rice — rougaille is always appropriate
The ginger is the Mauritian signature — it appears in no other 'rougaille' in the world
dinner.description: Mauritius' Creole base sauce — tomatoes broken down with onion, garlic, ginger, and thyme into a lightly spiced sauce that goes over everything: smoked sausages, fish, chicken, or rice. The fresh ginger is the Mauritian signature in rougaille — it appears in no equivalent sauce elsewhere in the French Creole world. Rougaille de saucisses (with smoked sausages) is the most beloved version.

dinner.name: Riz Frit Mauricien (Mauritius Fried Rice)
ingredients: Day-old rice (essential — fresh rice becomes soggy)
instructions: The key: day-old refrigerated rice — the rice dries out and fries properly
Fry garlic and ginger in hot oil
Add optional protein (shrimp, chicken, lap cheong sausage)
Add rice — fry over very high heat, pressing and tossing
Add soy sauce — it should smoke slightly and create a caramelized coating on the rice
Push rice aside, scramble eggs, mix through
Add spring onion, sesame oil
Mauritius fried rice is the Chinese-Creole hybrid — it has the Chinese fried rice technique
But rougaille spice or local flavors often creep in
It's served at Chinese restaurants, Chinese-Creole homes, and everywhere in between
dinner.description: Mauritius' fried rice — day-old rice fried over high heat with egg, soy sauce, and sesame oil in the Hakka Chinese technique. The Chinese community's most important contribution to Mauritian daily food. Often Chinese sausage (lap cheong) as the protein. The Chinese technique with occasional rougaille-influenced spicing is the Mauritius hybrid nature made edible.

dinner.name: Gateaux Piment (Chili Fritters)
ingredients: Fresh chili (generous — they should be spicy)
instructions: Grind soaked split peas coarsely — some whole, some broken
Add finely minced chili, garlic, fresh turmeric (not powder), cumin, spring onion
Season with salt
The mixture should be thick enough to hold a shape
Fry small flat cakes or rounds in hot oil
They should crisp on the outside — the pea starch forms a crust
Inside should be soft and spicy
Gateaux piment (chili cakes) are Mauritius' most iconic street food
Eaten at breakfast alongside dholl puri, or as snacks throughout the day
They're the Mauritian chili fritter — spicier than similar Indian preparations
The fresh turmeric (not powder) gives a floral, slightly bitter note
dinner.description: Mauritius' most iconic street snack — split pea fritters made spicy with generous fresh chili and fresh turmeric (the floral-bitter fresh note distinguishes them from dried-turmeric Indian versions). Eaten at breakfast alongside dholl puri or as snacks throughout the day. The gateaux piment seller at the bus stop is a Mauritius national image.

snacks.name: Gâteaux Piment (Chili Cakes)
instructions: Grind soaked peas coarsely
Mix with onion, chili, cumin, cilantro
Fry spoonfuls until golden

snacks.name: Gato Napolitaine (Jam Sandwich Cookie)
instructions: Make a sweet shortbread-type dough
Roll and cut into rounds (or rectangles)
Bake until lightly golden
Sandwich two together with jam filling
Dust with icing sugar
Gato napolitaine is Mauritius' colonial-era French pastry
The name suggests Neapolitan influence (French colonial connections to Italy through Europe)
It's become irreversibly Mauritian — found at every bakery and celebration
The simple jam sandwich cookie seems ordinary but has enormous cultural weight
It's the school snack, the Sunday treat, the family cookie tin item
The shortbread-jam combination is mild and sweet — comfort food for all communities
snacks.description: Mauritius' colonial-era jam sandwich cookie — shortbread rounds sandwiched with strawberry or pineapple jam, dusted with icing sugar. The French colonial legacy in biscuit form, now irreversibly Mauritian. The gato napolitaine is the cross-community food: Indian, Chinese, Creole, and Franco-Mauritian families all eat it. The school lunchbox cookie.

snacks.name: Ti Puri (Small Fried Bread)
ingredients: Salt, a pinch of baking powder
instructions: Mix flour, water, salt, baking powder into a soft dough
Shape into very small balls
Deep fry in oil until puffed and golden
Ti puri means 'small puri' in Mauritian Creole
The miniature fried bread is served with chutney and pickle
It's the snack version of dholl puri
Eaten at street stalls and home gatherings
Ti puri served with green chutney (coriander-chili) is a tea-time snack
The puffed, hollow interior collapses as you bite — steam escapes
The Indian puri adapted and miniaturized for Mauritian snacking contexts
snacks.description: Mauritius' miniature fried bread — tiny puri-sized dough balls deep-fried until puffed hollow, eaten with green chutney and pickle. The Indian puri adapted for snacking format. Ti puri with coriander-chili chutney is a Mauritius tea-time standard, crossing ethnic community lines completely.

snacks.name: Gato Arouille (Taro Cake)
instructions: Boil taro until very soft — drain well and mash
The taro must be dry — moisture makes it greasy when fried
Mix with garlic, spring onion, chili, salt, small amount of flour to bind
Shape into small flat cakes — the mixture is sticky
Fry until golden and crispy on the outside
The taro inside should be smooth and slightly earthy
Gato arouille is the Mauritius taro fritter — another Chinese-influenced adaptation
The Chinese brought taro preparation techniques; Mauritians added local spicing
Found at street stalls alongside gateaux piment
The taro's slightly sticky, earthy interior against the crispy exterior
snacks.description: Mauritius' taro fritter — boiled and mashed taro shaped into small cakes with garlic and chili, fried until crispy outside and smooth-earthy inside. Chinese taro preparation techniques adapted with Mauritian spicing. Taro has been a Pacific and Asian staple for thousands of years; in Mauritius it becomes a street fritter.

desserts.name: Napolitaine (Coconut Biscuit)
instructions: Make shortbread rounds
Top with jam
Cover with pink coconut icing
Let set
desserts.description: Iconic Mauritian layered biscuit — shortbread, jam, and pink coconut.

desserts.name: Napolitaine (Full Size)
ingredients: Pink royal icing (icing sugar, water, pink food coloring)
instructions: Make shortbread base
Bake until just firm
Sandwich with thick strawberry jam
Top with pink royal icing — this is the full Napolitaine
The pink icing is the visual signature of the full-size version
Let the icing set — it hardens over the jam
The combination: crumbly shortbread, sweet jam, hard pink icing
The Napolitaine is Mauritius' most sold cake — every bakery, every supermarket
It's the birthday cake layer option and the individually sold cake
The pink color is non-negotiable — white or other colors are not Napolitaine
desserts.description: Mauritius' most sold cake — shortbread sandwiched with strawberry jam and topped with pink royal icing, the icing's hardness creating a textural layer against the crumbly base. The pink color is non-negotiable and identity-defining: a Napolitaine without pink icing is not a Napolitaine. Found in every Mauritius bakery and supermarket. The national cake.

desserts.name: Ladoo (Indian Sweet Ball)
instructions: Toast chickpea flour in ghee over medium heat — stir constantly
Toast until the flour changes from raw to nutty — like toasted nut aroma
The toasting is the critical step — determines the flavor entirely
Remove from heat, cool slightly
Add powdered sugar, cardamom, optional raisins or cashews
While still warm, roll quickly into balls — the mixture holds together when warm
If it won't hold: add a little more ghee
Ladoo is Mauritius' Indian community celebration sweet — found at Diwali, weddings, Holi
The besan-ghee combination is ancient Indian sweet-making
In Mauritius, the Indian population (68%) has made ladoo part of the national celebration food
Ladoo is now eaten across all Mauritian communities at celebrations
desserts.description: Mauritius' Indian celebration sweet — chickpea flour toasted in ghee until nutty, mixed with sugar and cardamom while warm, rolled into balls. The toasting transforms raw flour into something deeply caramelized and nutty. Ladoo is the Diwali sweet, the wedding distribution, the Holi gift. India's 68% Mauritian community has made ladoo part of all Mauritian celebrations.

drinks.name: Alouda
instructions: Soak basil seeds, set agar jelly
Mix cold milk with sugar, vanilla, rose syrup
Add basil seeds and jelly cubes
Serve over ice
drinks.description: Mauritian milkshake with basil seeds and agar jelly.

drinks.name: Phoenix Beer
instructions: Serve cold in glass

drinks.name: Alouda (Milk and Basil Seed Drink)
ingredients: Basil seeds (sabja — soaked, they swell to 20x their size)
instructions: Soak basil seeds in cold water for 10 minutes — they swell dramatically into translucent gel spheres
The basil seeds look like tiny frog eggs — this is the visual signature
Mix cold milk with rose syrup (or vanilla syrup) — turns pink or vanilla-cream
Add basil seeds — they float and sink through the milk
Add crushed ice
Optional: agar jelly and vermicelli for additional texture
Alouda is Mauritius' most iconic drink — found at every street stall
The basil seed gel texture in cold sweet milk is unlike any other drink
Brought by the Indian community — similar drinks exist in India and South Asia
But alouda as sold in Mauritius (with the dramatic basil seed gel spheres) is distinctly Mauritian
drinks.description: Mauritius' most iconic drink — cold sweet milk with rose syrup and basil seeds (sabja) that have swollen into dramatic translucent gel spheres. The visual of gel spheres floating in pink milk is the Mauritius alouda image. A South Asian import adapted by the Indian community into something distinctly Mauritius: every street stall sells it, all communities drink it.
